image.caption: Florida State University students attend a candlelight vigil on campus after the shooting of three FSU students earlier Thursday in Tallahassee, Fla. About 3,000 students attended the vigil.

Residents clear snow from a porch roof while leaning from a second-story window in Buffalo, N.Y., on Friday. A snowfall that brought huge drifts and closed roads in the Buffalo area finally ended, replaced with the looming threat of rain and higher temperatures through the weekend that could cause flooding and roof collapses.

The Capitol Christmas tree is set upright on the West Front of the U.S. Capitol Friday in Washington, D.C. The tree, an approximately 88-foot tall white pine, is a gift from the state of Minnesota and was harvested from the Chippewa National Forest.

Indonesian President Joko Widodo, popularly known as "Jokowi," center, and his wife Iriana, center left, take a selfie after attending the graduation ceremony of son Kaesang Pangarep, top right, at the Anglo-Chinese School in Singapore on Friday.
Relatives and friends attend the funeral ceremony of Spain’s Duchess of Alba, Maria del Rosario Cayetana Fitz-James Stuart y Silva, at the cathedral in Seville, Spain, on Friday.
Secretary of State John Kerry leaves Palais Coburg, where closed-door nuclear talks with Iran are taking place, in Vienna, Austria, on Friday.

Federal police spray protesters with fire extinguishers as they drive them back from the National Palace in Mexico City on Thursday. Protesters marched in the capital city to demand authorities find 43 missing college students.

A surfer goes airborne as he rides a big wave during a tow-in surfing session in Nazare, Portugal, on Thursday. A tow-in is a surf technique in which the athlete is towed into a large wave by a partner driving a Jet Ski or other watercraft with an attached line.
A Palestinian woman flinches as Israeli border policemen clash with protesters at the Qalandia checkpoint near the West Bank city of Ramallah on Friday.

Lit candles form the coat of arms of Ukraine in Kiev's Independence Square on Friday. Ukraine marked the first anniversary of demonstrations known as Euromaidan, which were sparked by then-President Viktor Yanukovych's decision to tilt away from the West and toward Moscow. The protests drew hundreds of thousands, leading to a bloody crackdown by security forces in late February and the eventual ouster of Yanukovych as he fled to neighboring Russia.

webpage.text:
Why I boycotted Congress' 'moment of silence' after the Texas shooting

Like many Americans, I watched in horror as the news rolled in this past weekend about the mass shooting unfolding at a church in Texas. My heart broke at the stories of children and parishioners gunned down in their place of worship. I cannot begin to imagine the pain and dread the loved ones of the victims must feel — from classrooms in Sandy Hook to concerts in Las Vegas, it feels like no place is safe from mass shootings anymore.

And as a Catholic, I did pray for the victims and their families that day. But as a federal legislator, I know our thoughts and prayers are simply not enough.

When tragedy strikes, feeling helpless is understandable. There is little you can do to stop a tornado, a hurricane, or a cancer diagnosis from changing your life in an instant. But gun violence is not an unavoidable fact of life.

We cannot treat Sunday’s events as a natural disaster — this tragedy is man-made. We know this because around the world, our peers in government and law enforcement do not pretend to be helpless. Indeed, other civilized countries have done a far better job at reducing gun violence. Offering thoughts and prayers are a valuable way to let loved ones know you care, but no one should offer them at the expense of action.

That’s why when Speaker Paul Ryan asked for yet another moment of silence in the U.S. Capitol on Monday, I chose to leave.

I respect my colleagues who participate in moments of silence. I have participated in all of them until now. But based on the increasing number of mass shootings and the inaction of Congress, I have concluded that the best way to honor victims of mass shootings is to try to prevent future mass shootings, not stand and be silent for 60 seconds.

Since I became a member of Congress in 2015, there have been over 1,000 mass shootings in the United States according to the nonprofit Gun Violence Archive, including three of the most deadly in U.S. history.

Since I became a member of Congress in 2015, more than 60,000 people have died from firearms-related deaths in the United States, according to the Centers for Disease Control.

Since I became a member of Congress in 2015, Congress has not taken a single vote on gun safety legislation.

But since 2015 we did hold a number of 60-second moments of silence — more than 20, actually. And what have those 60 second acts resulted in? Nothing.

brut.title: FSU Shooter Myron May Left Message: 'I Do Not Want to Die in ...

webpage.text:
FSU Shooter Myron May Left Message: 'I Do Not Want to Die in Vain'

Hours before he opened fire at the Florida State University library, lawyer Myron May left a desperate voicemail for an acquaintance with this plea: "I do not want to die in vain."

The message was part of a flurry of emails, texts and phone calls in which the former prosecutor laid bare his torment: He believed government "stalkers" were harassing him and using a "direct energy weapon" to hurt him. He said that he had sent packages to 10 people that would "expose" what he thought was happening to him.


Police have said that May, 31, a Florida State graduate, was in a paranoia-fueled "state of crisis" when he showed up to the library with a .380 semiautomic pistol, shot three people and was then killed by cops when he would not drop the weapon.

His social media activity revealed that he believed he was a "targeted individual," the term used by people who think the government and shadowy gangs are attacking them with mind control and invisible, remote weapons.

Renee Pittman Mitchell, who calls herself a "targeted individual" and has a website devoted to those claims, said May reached out to her through Facebook about a week ago in anguish.

"He told me he just didn't want to go on living like this," Mitchell said. She said that after their initial conversations, she became wary of May, concerned that he might be what she called an "impostor." May continued to try to contact her and left three voicemails between 9:19 p.m. and 9:42 p.m. ET Wednesday, she said.

"I am currently being cooked in my chair. I devised a scheme where I was going to expose this once and for all and I really need you," he said in one of the messages, which was provided to NBC News and authenticated by a relative as May's voice. "I do not want to die in vain."

In an email he sent at 11:19 p.m., he wrote: "I've been getting hit with the direct energy weapon in my chest all evening. It hurts really bad right now." Police say he opened fire on campus about an hour later.


It is unclear when May’s mental distress began. A graduate of FSU and the Texas Tech law school, he practiced law in Texas and New Mexico, where he worked as a prosecutor for the Dona Ana district attorney’s office until he abruptly quit Oct. 6.

The next night, May’s ex-girlfriend called Las Cruces police to report that he had showed up at her home, rambling. She told the officer that May had been diagnosed with ADHD and was taking medication for it but had recently “developed a severe mental disorder,” the police report said.

“Myron believes that the police are after him and are bugging his phone and car as well as placing cameras in his home and car,” the report said. She said he had been up without sleep for four or five days straight.

She said he had not made any threats to hurt himself or others but had been evaluated at a local hospital two weeks earlier.

The ex-girlfriend’s call was not the first time May drew police attention. On Sept. 7, he showed up at the police station to report that someone had planted a camera in his house. “He stated that he can constantly hear voices coming through the walls specifically talking about the actions he was doing,” the officer wrote in his report.

May returned to Florida, where he had lived with his grandmother as a teenager, in late October. He was staying with a family friend until last Friday, when he left and didn’t return.

In subsequent days, he made several posts on a Facebook page for “Targeted Individuals International,” including one that asked, “Has anyone here ever been encouraged by your handler to kill with a promise of freedom?”

An email he sent Mitchell hours before the library shootings outlined 10 packages he had sent to her and other friends around the country, with photos of certified mail receipts and tracking information. Mitchell said she had not yet received the package, but had been told it contained videos and writing on a thumb drive.

In one of the text messages, he said he was sending return receipts for the packages to Mitchell “because I anticipate that I’ll be gone at that point.”

webpage.text:
Florida State quest to win second straight national title interrupted by sobering reality of school shooting – New York Daily News

There wasn’t even a whole month between school shootings this time, more innocent kids discovering that their own Second Amendment right was the right to run when somebody starts to shoot, in a country lousy with guns. This time it happened at Florida State, which is supposed to be about football at this time of year, all the second-half comebacks and 26 wins in a row and FSU trying to win a second straight national championship.

But then the famous football school became famous for another school shooting, as kids there were getting ready for exams and then Florida State against Boston College, the big television game on Saturday afternoon.

Then they weren’t talking about Jameis Winston trying to win another Heisman Trophy or another title, or bad behavior that got him suspended for a game. Or about what had previously been the big story about a crime there, a hit-and-run accident involving a couple of FSU cornerbacks that resulted in only a couple of tickets. Instead in Tallahassee they were talking about a man who pulled out a gun and started shooting at a campus library.

Florida State’s thrilling football season then became part of the school-shooting season in America, one that never seems to end.

It was a handgun at the Strozier Library. That made it much more challenging for the shooter to hit moving targets. History shows that it is a lot easier for the shooter when he’s got some kind of automatic weapon to make the killing or even the chance at killing innocent people a lot easier and faster.

So at a little after midnight Thursday in a college library, the place where college kids go to learn and dream or sometimes just go looking for some quiet, the quiet at Florida State was shattered by gunfire, those inside running upstairs and into stacks of books not to study or learn but trying to find safety from a madman with a gun. It turned out that some of them were saved by backpacks and books.

And in those moments of terror, nobody knowing how many people had been hit or if the shooter was going to keep coming the way other shooters had at other schools, we had another school in this country that was not safe, four weeks after the last time it happened like this in Washington state.

For now there are no fatalities at Florida State. It was much worse and much deadlier on Oct. 24 at Marysville Pilchuck (Wash.) High School when a 15-year-old freshman football player named Jaylen Fryberg shot five of his fellow students, killing four of them. It was the cafeteria at Fryberg’s high school that day. It was a library at the college in Tallahassee famous for football until an alumnus named Myron May started firing away.

So May joined all the other school shooters in this country, just in the years since Columbine High School. May just didn’t have a good enough killing gun, the way Adam Lanza did when he went hunting for first graders at Sandy Hook Elementary. Or maybe this guy just wasn’t a good enough shot before the cops shot him dead and saved the lives of college kids and library workers, on the night when they all went from library quiet to being in a shooting gallery.

“Mr. May was in a state of crisis . . . struggling either psychologically or emotionally,” Michael DeLeo, the chief of the Tallahassee Police Department, said afterward.

Once again you will hear that this isn’t about the gun in May’s hand, or guns at all, that this is only about mental illness. But every time you hear that, both from sensible gun owners and the gun nuts from the National Rifle Association, you want to ask them if this is only a crisis of mental health, how come other civilized countries don’t have gun violence killing 86 people a day the way it does in this country?

It was a high school cafeteria in Washington state on Oct. 24, this Fryberg ambushing family members and friends. Now it is a college library in Florida in the early moments of Nov. 20. It’s as if we are back on schedule now. Another big year for this kind of shooting. Six months ago, almost exactly, a big shooting spree started at the University of California, Santa Barbara.

This is part of an eloquent statement Thursday from Shannon Watts, the founder of Moms Demand Action for Gun Sense in America:

“As the parent of a college student, I know how hard it is to send your child to college — you want to imagine them studying in the library, not crouching in the stacks to hide from a gunman, as we know the students at FSU did last night. Events like this should be a call to action for our political leaders to address the gun violence that has resulted in nearly 100 school shootings since the Sandy Hook tragedy. That’s why Moms Demand Action was started and that’s why we’ll keep fighting for common sense public safety measures that can help prevent tragedies like this one.”

Shouting at the political leaders Watts references, though, is the same as shouting to be heard over the sound of another gun going off at another school. It is a shame of our country how we are no longer surprised when it happens again. If one kid is at risk, all of them are.

The great cowards of American political life are the elected officials who run from these mutts in the gun lobby the way kids ran from Myron May at Florida State. The President just talks about guns, Congress just talks, the only major politician with any guts on this subject continues to be Michael Bloomberg.

This time the latest school shooting comes before a big football Saturday afternoon in Tallahassee, a week before Thanksgiving. Maybe we get another one in time for Christmas. This is a season that never ends.
